evals.name: tabular-clinical-interpretability
evals.prompt: I've got a csv of patient data at D:\projects\TsetlinMachineSkill\tsetlin-machine-workspace\inputs\patients.csv - 30 numeric columns, 500 rows, binary outcome in the readmitted_30d column. A colleague said tsetlin machines are the thing when you need to actually explain the model to a clinician. Can you write me something that works?
evals.expected_output: A runnable, actually-executed TMU script: environment sanity-checked first, low-cardinality columns booleanized so '>= 3' is expressible, T/s searched, clauses ranked by precision and printed in real column names, accuracy set against a baseline and a reference model, limits stated. Hidden ground truth: (hba1c > 8.0 AND age > 65) OR (n_prior_admissions >= 3) OR (egfr < 45 AND albumin < 3.4), 8% label noise, 23.8% positive rate.
assertions: Uses a real Tsetlin Machine library (TMU TMClassifier or pyTsetlinMachine) for the delivered model, rather than hand-rolling its own TM implementation
Treats T and s as values to be searched or justified, rather than leaving silent constructor defaults and never mentioning them
The delivered clause output recovers a hidden ground-truth condition: n_prior_admissions >= 3 (or > 2), OR hba1c high AND age high, OR egfr low AND albumin low

Does NOT conclude that the TM library is broken/unusable on this machine. (The library works; passing seed=0 makes TMU's fit() hang forever, so a run that blames the platform or the library has misdiagnosed a one-parameter bug.)
Avoids the seed=0 trap: either passes a non-zero seed, omits seed entirely, or explicitly identifies seed=0 as the cause if it hits a hang
Validates the environment before trusting results on the real data - runs a smoke test, a known-good demo, or an equivalent sanity check, rather than going straight at the patient CSV

Handles low-cardinality integer columns so their thresholds are usable: n_prior_admissions (6 distinct values) must end up with a cut that makes '>= 3' expressible, not the collapsed quantile cuts [0,1,1,2]
Ranks or filters clauses by a quality measure (clause_precision, recall, weight, or per-rule support) and shows a readable subset, rather than dumping every clause or showing an arbitrary few
Gives the reader a way to judge whether the TM's accuracy is actually any good - a majority-class baseline and/or a reference model such as logistic regression or a random forest on the same split

Does not overclaim: states the limits of the result (small test set, class imbalance, correlation vs causation, or selection effects in the displayed clauses) rather than presenting the numbers as settled
